results.summary: This is a simple design created during the TinyTapeout workshop. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, but the documentation does not describe any specific function. The design is likely intended as a learning exercise or template. No external hardware or testing procedure is mentioned.

This project implements a flip-flop with set, reset, and enable inputs. The outputs provide both the stored value and its complement. To test it, the inputs should be pulled high via resistors and then momentarily grounded using buttons to change state. External hardware includes four resistors, two LEDs, and two buttons.

This is a simple test project described as just experimenting a bit. It has two inputs and three outputs, but the documentation states that twiddling the inputs causes something arbitrary to happen at the outputs. No specific function or external hardware is described. The design is not intended for any particular application.

This design is a 4-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register with an output enable. Data is shifted in on the clock edge, and the parallel outputs are only active when the output enable is high. It can be tested by providing a clock and data input, and observing the outputs with LEDs. External hardware requires four LEDs for the outputs.

This project creates configurable spinning animations on a 7-segment display. The animation mode and direction are selected via an 8-pin DIP switch, and the decimal point can show the clock pulse. It requires a 7-segment display, DIP switch, reset switch, and clock input for testing. The design is notable for its use of a 4 Hz clock and multiple animation patterns.

This project implements a D flip-flop with clock and data inputs, and both Q and Q' outputs. It can be tested manually by connecting a clock signal and a button to the data input, and observing the outputs with LEDs. External hardware includes a clock source, a button, and two LEDs. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand the basic function.

This design is a 4-bit synchronous counter with a fully decoded hex output for a 7-segment display. It uses 29 2-input NAND gates for decoding, based on a minimized design from Kim Oyhus. The counter has an active-high enable and asynchronous reset, and counts on the positive clock edge. It requires no external hardware beyond the standard demo board.

This project displays numbers 1 through 8 on a 7-segment display based on which of eight switches is turned on. The decimal point is connected to the clock to visualize its operation. It is tested by simply toggling the input switches. External hardware required is a 7-segment display.

This design blinks the number 7 on a 7-segment display using a single AND gate and an oscillator. The blinking is activated by a high signal on input 6. It is tested by turning on switch 7. External hardware includes a 7-segment display.

This project consists of some logic gates intended for mask production testing. The documentation explicitly states it should not be used at all. It has four inputs and four outputs, and testing would involve connecting LEDs to the outputs. The design is not meant for any functional application.
